cases.lesson: Storing sensitive data insecurely and hiding a breach is the fastest way to become the example.
cases.what: The first settlement under DOJ's Civil Cyber-Fraud Initiative. CHS failed to provide adequate cybersecurity for medical data supporting State Department and Air Force operations, stored sensitive personal information insecurely, and failed to disclose a breach.

cases.lesson: Years of misrepresented compliance, uncovered by an employee whistleblower, became a $9 million lesson in taking self-assessments seriously.
cases.what: One of the initiative's first major cases. The aerospace and defense contractor allegedly misrepresented its cybersecurity compliance to DoD and NASA for years while continuing to bid on and win contracts. The case began as a whistleblower (qui tam) suit by a former employee.

cases.lesson: Small businesses are not too small for enforcement. If you host a federally funded system, you own its security.
cases.what: A graphic design firm that failed to provide and maintain secure hosting for HealthyKids.org, a federally funded website handling children's health insurance information.

cases.lesson: Self-disclosure and cooperation cut the penalty multiplier from 3x to 1.5x, saving Verizon over $1.3 million. Finding it yourself beats DOJ finding it.
cases.what: Verizon's own compliance review found issues with security controls on its Managed Trusted Internet Protocol Services for federal agencies. It self-reported to the GSA Inspector General, cooperated, and earned a reduced 1.5x penalty multiplier instead of treble damages.

cases.lesson: Data you collect under a government contract is data you must protect. Losing control of it is a false claim, not just an IT incident.
cases.what: The staffing company failed to keep health information obtained during COVID-19 contact tracing for the Pennsylvania Department of Health confidential and secure.

cases.lesson: If the contract requires pre-production security testing, skipping it and billing anyway is fraud, not a shortcut.
cases.what: The consulting firm failed to conduct contractually required pre-production cybersecurity testing on New York State's Emergency Rental Assistance Program technology.

cases.lesson: Subcontractors face the same exposure as primes when the security requirement flows down to them.
cases.what: Guidehouse's subcontractor on the same Emergency Rental Assistance Program work, settled alongside the prime for the same testing failures.

cases.lesson: Falsely certifying compliance in annual reports for three years, while your own auditors warn you, is the textbook FCA case.
cases.what: HNFS falsely certified compliance with cybersecurity requirements in its TRICARE contract with the Defense Health Agency from 2015 to 2018, failed to scan for vulnerabilities on time, and ignored warnings from third-party auditors and its own internal audit team.

cases.lesson: Your SPRS score is evidence. Posting 104 when a third-party assessment says -142, and never correcting it, is exactly what DOJ prosecutes.
cases.what: The Cambridge defense contractor admitted it had not fully implemented NIST 800-171 controls, posted an inflated SPRS self-assessment score of 104 (a later third-party assessment found -142), had no system security plan for some systems, and used email hosting that did not meet the FedRAMP Moderate baseline.

cases.lesson: Buyers inherit the target's compliance history. Nightwing paid for cybersecurity failures that happened before it bought the business.
cases.what: Raytheon failed to develop a required system security plan and failed to implement required cybersecurity controls on systems supporting 29 DoD contracts and subcontracts from 2015 to 2021. Nightwing, which later acquired the business, assumed liability as successor. The whistleblower, a former Raytheon engineering director, received about $1.5 million.

cases.lesson: A self-assessment score must describe a real system. Scoring a fictitious environment 98 out of 110 fooled no one.
cases.what: The university's Astrolab ran DoD cyber-defense research with no antivirus tools installed and no system security plan, then submitted a campus-wide SPRS score of 98 based on what DOJ called a fictitious environment. Two whistleblowers from Georgia Tech's own cybersecurity team split $201,250.

cases.lesson: Acquiring a defense contractor means acquiring its compliance history. Due diligence must include cybersecurity representations.
cases.what: Settlement resolving allegations tied to a defense contractor's cybersecurity compliance history, with liability extending to the acquiring private equity owner.

cases.lesson: The first FCA cyber settlement over medical device software, with no breach alleged. Knowing about a severe vulnerability and staying silent was enough.
cases.what: The genetic testing company allegedly failed to disclose or remediate a severe cybersecurity vulnerability in its software that was identified by a third party. The first cyber FCA settlement focused on medical device cybersecurity requirements.

cases.lesson: No whistleblower needed. A government DIBCAC assessment scored LOGZONE at -170 after it self-reported 110, and the assessment itself became the case.
cases.what: The Huntsville defense contractor posted a perfect 110 self-assessment in 2021 for two Navy contracts. A 2024 government assessment scored it at -170. Restitution alone exceeded one-third of what the contracts had paid.

cases.lesson: Billing the government for years while failing NIST 800-171 on your own network turns an IT gap into a false claim. The whistleblower received $375,823.
cases.what: Honeywell failed to comply with NIST SP 800-171 safeguarding requirements on one of its networks from 2020 through 2023 while continuing to bill under defense contracts. The case began as a whistleblower suit by a former employee.

meta.note: Announced settlements with individual sources below. Not exhaustive: DOJ announces new matters over time, and some totals cited in commentary aggregate differently. Amounts are settlement figures, not admissions of liability unless noted.
